I'm new to reading budget-vs-actual reports. What should I actually look at first?

Look at two rankings, not one, because they answer different questions.

First, rank by absolute variance — the dollar gap between actual and budget. That's where the money went. If catering was budgeted at $4,800 and came in at $5,520, the variance is +$720: real money that has to come from somewhere.

Second, rank by percentage variance — the gap divided by the budget. That tells you where the plan itself was wrong. Supplies budgeted at $900 and spent at $610 show a variance of -$290, which is -32.2% — a small dollar amount, but the budget for that line was clearly built on a wrong assumption, and next year's budget will inherit the error if nobody asks why.

A line like rent — $3,500 budgeted, $3,500 spent, zero variance on both rankings — needs no attention at all.

Then, for each line that ranks high on either list, ask one question: is this a one-off or a new rate of spending? A one-off (a repair, an event) explains the past. A new rate (a price rise, a changed habit) predicts the future, and it's the second kind that should change your next budget. Finally, treat big underspends with the same suspicion as overspends: money not spent usually means work not done, which surfaces later as a different problem.

My department came in well under budget this year and my manager is thrilled. Should I be?

Only if the work the money was for actually got done. An underspend is a difference between a plan and reality, and there are three very different reasons it happens.

The genuinely good reason: you found a cheaper way to deliver the same output — a renegotiated contract, a process that stopped wasting material. That saving repeats and should be banked into next year's budget.

The neutral reason: something outside your control didn't happen. A role budgeted at $68,000 sat vacant for five months, so the salary line is far under — but the team's workload didn't shrink, it was absorbed as overtime and delay elsewhere. The saving is real on that line and fictional for the department.

The bad reason: the work silently didn't occur. A training budget of $12,000 with only $4,300 spent often means two courses were cancelled, not that training got cheaper — the $7,700 'saving' is a capability gap that shows up later as errors and attrition. Deferred maintenance is the classic version: this year's underspend becomes next year's emergency repair at a multiple of the cost.

So before celebrating, walk the big underspent lines and sort each into delivered-cheaper, didn't-happen-externally, or didn't-happen-and-will-cost-us. Your manager's delight is justified for the first pile only — and if most of the underspend is in the third pile, the honest move is to say so now, while it's still a planning conversation rather than a post-mortem.

We investigate every budget line that's more than 10% off, and it's too many false alarms and still misses big stuff. How should we set the threshold?

A percentage-only rule fails at both ends, because percentage ignores size. Consider two lines from the same quarter:

- Line A: budget $200,000, actual $206,000. Variance +3% — your rule ignores it, yet $6,000 of unplanned spend just walked past.
- Line B: budget $800, actual $1,300. Variance +62.5% — your rule triggers an investigation over $500, which may be one mistimed invoice.

Use a two-part materiality test instead: investigate when a line is off by at least $1,000 in absolute terms, OR off by at least 15% AND at least $750. Run the examples through it: Line A qualifies on dollars alone (+$6,000), which is correct — that's real money regardless of the small percentage. Line B fails both tests (+$500), so it waits unless it repeats. A third line — budget $4,000, actual $4,900, which is +$900 and +22.5% — qualifies under the second test: too big proportionally to be noise, and $900 is enough to matter.

Two refinements make it work in practice. First, calibrate the dollar floors to your scale: a common starting point is roughly 0.5–1% of the total budget as the absolute floor. Second, add a persistence rule: a line that misses the threshold but is off in the same direction three periods running gets investigated anyway, because a small, steady drift is a changed spending rate announcing itself quietly. The goal is a short list where every item is worth a conversation — not the longest list you can generate.

What's the actual difference between a budget and a cash-flow projection? My accountant keeps using them like they're different things.

They are different things, and confusing them causes real mistakes.

A budget is a plan for amounts over a period: we intend to spend $60,000 on wages this quarter and earn $95,000 in sales. It doesn't care when within the quarter the money moves. A budget answers 'how much, in total?'

A cash-flow projection is a timeline of your bank balance: it cares about the order and the dates. It answers 'on our worst day, how much is actually in the account?' A business can hit its budget exactly and still bounce a payment, because the $95,000 of sales might be invoiced in month one and paid in month three, while the $60,000 of wages leaves every Friday.

Two habits make projections trustworthy. First, project receipts when cash arrives, not when invoices are issued — those are different months for most businesses. Second, write the assumptions on the projection itself ('receipts at last year's level, costs up 3%, no new hires'). A projection without stated assumptions can't be argued with, which sounds convenient and is actually useless: when reality disagrees, you can't tell which assumption broke, so you learn nothing for next time.

Rule of thumb: budget for the year, project cash for the next thirteen weeks, and review the projection against the actual bank balance every week. The budget judges your plan; the projection protects your balance.

Our cash-flow projection said we'd be fine last month and we still nearly missed payroll. The totals for the month were about right. What went wrong?

If the monthly totals were about right but payroll nearly failed, you had a timing error, not an amount error — and projections built from monthly totals are blind to it.

Here's the classic shape. A client owes you $12,000. Your projection books it in the month the invoice is issued, on 30-day terms. The client actually pays on day 60. Meanwhile your outgoings are $9,500 a month, every month, starting from a balance of $7,000. On paper the month closes fine: 7,000 + 12,000 - 9,500 = 9,500. In the bank, the sequence is 7,000 - 9,500 = -2,500 before the receipt ever lands. The totals agree with reality; the calendar doesn't, and payroll is a calendar event.

Three fixes, in order of value. First, project receipts at expected payment date, not invoice date — use each customer's actual payment history if you have it, because '30-day terms' is a hope, not a schedule. Second, project weekly instead of monthly for the next 13 weeks; timing errors live inside months. Third, track the projected lowest point of the balance, not the month-end figure: the low point is what your credit line or reserve has to cover.

The lesson to keep: a projection can be right about every amount and still get you in trouble. Accuracy about when is worth as much as accuracy about how much.

Because month-end is the most flattering day of the month to look at, and cash problems happen on other days.

Walk through a typical month with round numbers. You start with $3,200. Rent of $2,600 leaves on the 5th: $600. Payroll of $8,400 lands on the 15th: you're at -$7,800. Your customers pay on the 28th — $9,800 arrives and you close the month at +$2,000. Every month-end snapshot says +$2,000 and 'fine'. For thirteen days in the middle, you were nearly eight thousand short, and that's when the bookkeeper is sweating: one early supplier demand or one late customer in that window and a payment bounces.

The fix is to manage the low point, not the average. Three concrete habits: project cash weekly so the mid-month trough is a number you know in advance, not a surprise; line up your outflows against your inflows where you can (moving a supplier payment from the 12th to the 29th costs nothing and flattens the trough); and size any credit line to the trough — here, at least $7,800 of headroom, not the $2,000 the month-end figure might suggest.

Profit is a monthly total; cash is a daily sequence. Your bookkeeper is watching the sequence.

Per drink: ingredients and cup come to $1.63, labor is $0.75 (3 minutes at $15/hour), so variable cost is $2.38 and each drink contributes $3.12 toward fixed costs.

The margin above break-even is thinner than the daily number feels: five fewer drinks a day — one rainy week — puts you back at break-even. And note what this excludes: the truck's depreciation and your own pay beyond the labor rate are not in the $2,340, so treat the $418.08 as the pot those come out of, not as take-home profit.
People keep using contribution margin, gross margin, and profit like they're the same number. They're not, are they?

They're not — they answer three different questions, and mixing them up produces bad pricing decisions. Take one product: it sells for $50. Materials are $18, direct labor $9, and the selling platform takes $5 per sale.

Contribution margin subtracts every cost that happens because this one unit sold: 50 - 18 - 9 - 5 = $18 per unit (36% of the price). It answers: 'if I sell one more, how much better off am I?' That's the number break-even runs on — with $9,000 a month of fixed costs, you need 9,000 / 18 = 500 units before the business covers its costs.

Gross margin subtracts only the cost of making the product — here materials plus labor, $27 — giving $23 (46%). It answers 'how much room is there above production cost?' It's the number accountants report, but it hides per-sale costs like the platform's $5, which is why a product can show a healthy gross margin and still lose money on every incremental sale through an expensive channel.

Profit subtracts everything, including fixed costs that don't vary with units — rent, insurance, salaries. Profit answers 'did the business make money this period?' and it depends on volume in a way the other two don't: the same product at 400 units loses money and at 600 units makes it, with identical margins.

Working rule: price and channel decisions with contribution, report with gross margin, judge the period with profit — and never let one number do another's job.

We hit our break-even unit target last quarter and still lost money. How is that possible?

Because break-even in units silently assumes a sales mix, and your mix moved. Break-even isn't a property of your fixed costs alone — it's fixed costs divided by the average contribution per unit, and the average depends on what you actually sell.

Say you have two products: A contributes $12 a unit, B contributes $5. Fixed costs are $6,300 a month. At a 50/50 mix the average contribution is $8.50, so break-even is about 742 units. Now suppose the mix shifts to 25% A and 75% B — perhaps B is the one on promotion. Average contribution falls to $6.75 and break-even rises to about 934 units.

Sell 800 units — comfortably above the 'target' of 742 — and the two worlds diverge: at the old mix, 800 units contribute $6,800, which is $500 of profit. At the new mix they contribute $5,400, which is a $900 loss. Same units, same fixed costs, opposite result. Nothing went wrong in your counting; the target itself was computed for a mix you no longer sell.

The defenses are simple. State break-even as a mix ('742 units at 50/50') rather than a bare number, recompute it when the mix shifts materially, and if one product dominates your promotions, compute break-even at the promotional mix before the campaign, not after the quarter. Units are the denominator everyone watches; mix is the assumption nobody writes down.

I tutor through a platform. Sessions are one hour at $65. The platform takes 20%. Travel costs me about $6.50 a session and materials $1.25. My fixed costs (insurance, software, a bit of advertising) are $265 a month. I currently do 14 sessions a month. Am I actually making money?
Working out the per-session contribution and comparing it with your fixed costs at current volume.

Per session: the platform takes $13, so of the $65 you keep $52 before your own costs; minus travel and materials the contribution is $44.25 a session.

Break-even is 6 sessions a month — 5 sessions contribute $221.25, which doesn't cover the $265, and 6 contribute $265.50, which just does. At your current 14 sessions you're contributing $619.5, leaving $354.5 a month after fixed costs. So yes, you're making money — roughly two and a third times your break-even volume.

Two honest caveats. First, that $354.5 is before paying yourself for the hour itself: the $65 buys the student's outcome, and your teaching time is compensated out of the contribution, so your effective hourly rate after all costs is closer to the contribution than to $65. Second, travel is your softest number — if a session across town really costs $11 in fuel and parking rather than $6.50, contribution drops to $39.75 and break-even rises to 7 sessions. Still comfortably below 14, but worth one month of actual receipts before you quote the $44.25 figure anywhere.
Our costing spreadsheet allocates fixed overhead per unit and one product keeps flipping between 'profitable' and 'unprofitable' depending on the month's volume. Is the product actually a problem?

Almost certainly not — the spreadsheet is. Allocated unit cost has volume baked into it, so it manufactures exactly the flipping you describe.

Run the mechanics. Fixed overhead is $20,000 a month and the product's variable cost is $30. In a 1,000-unit month, allocation adds $20 a unit: full cost $50. In a 700-unit month it adds $28.57: full cost $58.57. In a 2,000-unit month it adds $10: full cost $40. The product didn't change; the denominator did. Price it at $60 and it looks healthy in good months and marginal in bad ones, purely as an accounting artifact.

Worse, the artifact can drive a death spiral. Price from the 1,000-unit full cost, add a margin, and if the resulting price suppresses volume to 700, the recomputed cost rises, the product 'fails' its review, and it gets cut — even though every unit sold contributed $30 above variable cost toward the fixed $20,000, and cutting it means the remaining products must absorb that $20,000 between fewer units.

Use the two numbers for their proper jobs. Contribution ($30 a unit here, price minus variable cost) decides whether to sell, promote, or drop something. Fully-allocated cost is a reporting convention for valuing inventory and comparing periods — legitimate on a financial statement, dangerous in a pricing meeting. If a product's contribution is positive and it isn't crowding out something better, it is paying rent, whatever the allocation says this month.

When revenue changes, people say 'it's price' or 'it's volume'. How do you actually separate the two?

With a simple convention: measure the price effect at the new quantity, and the volume effect at the old price. The two sum exactly to the revenue change.

Example. A market stall sells mugs: price rises from $10 to $11, and quantity falls from 100 to 90. Revenue moves from $1,000 to $990 — down $10.

Price effect: the $1 increase, applied to the 90 mugs actually sold: +$90. Volume effect: the 10 mugs not sold, valued at the old $10 price: -$100. Total: 90 - 100 = -$10, which is the whole change, with nothing left over.

The reading: the price rise earned $90 and the volume it cost lost $100 — the rise was (narrowly) a mistake on revenue terms. Without the split, all you'd know is 'revenue dipped slightly after we raised prices', which supports almost any opinion.

Two cautions. First, the split depends on the convention — valuing the price effect at the old quantity instead gives +$100 and -$110. Same total, slightly different story. Pick one convention, state it, and use it consistently. Second, revenue decomposition says nothing about profit: if the 10 lost mug sales were your most expensive to serve, the 'mistake' might have raised profit. Decompose revenue to understand demand; decompose contribution to make decisions.

Our materials spend was way over budget this month and the report calls it 'unfavorable'. But we also sold way more than planned. Is the label fair?

Probably not, and the reason is a classic variance trap: comparing actual spend with a budget built for a different volume of output.

Put numbers on it. The plan assumed 1,000 units, each using 2 kg of material at $4.20/kg — a materials budget of $8,400. You actually made 1,200 units and used 2,460 kg, costing $10,332. Against the static budget that's $1,932 'over' — unfavorable, in red, demanding explanation.

But most of that gap is just success. Producing 1,200 units should use 2,400 kg by the standard. You used 2,460 — only 60 kg of genuine excess, worth $252. The other $1,680 of the 'overrun' is the material content of the 200 extra units you sold, which arrived with revenue attached. A variance system that punishes that is punishing the sales team for selling.

The fix is a flexible budget: restate the standard at the actual output level (1,200 units → $10,080 of standard material cost) and judge the floor against that. Your real performance question shrinks to the honest $252 — was the extra 60 kg scrap, a quality input, or measurement noise?

Labels worth keeping: 'unfavorable' should mean 'worse than it should have been for what we actually did', never merely 'more than we guessed in January'.

Two analysts decomposed the same revenue change for me and got completely different price and volume effects. One of them must have made an error, right?

Probably neither. They likely used different conventions, and the difference between conventions is a real quantity with a name: the interaction term.

Take a stark case: price rises from $10 to $14 while quantity falls from 100 to 60. Revenue falls from $1,000 to $840, a change of -$160.

Analyst A values the price effect at the new quantity and volume at the old price: price = 4 x 60 = +$240, volume = -40 x 10 = -$400. Sum: -$160.

Analyst B does the reverse: price = 4 x 100 = +$400, volume = -40 x 14 = -$560. Sum: also -$160.

Both totals are right; the splits differ by $160 in each component. That $160 is the interaction: the price rise applied to the units no longer sold (4 x -40 = -$160). It belongs to neither effect cleanly — it exists because price and quantity moved together — and each convention quietly assigns it to a different side.

The professional fixes are threefold. State the convention next to the numbers, every time. Use one convention consistently across periods so trends are comparable. And when the interaction is large relative to the effects — as here, where it's as big as the total change — report it as its own line: price +$400, volume -$400, interaction -$160. That third presentation is the honest one when both levers moved hard at once, because a decomposition that hides a third of the story inside an arbitrary assignment will eventually be 'wrong' in exactly the way your two analysts just demonstrated.

People keep telling me to 'backtest' a forecast before trusting it. What does that actually involve?

It means making the method forecast the past — a past it wasn't allowed to see — and scoring how wrong it was. Only then do you let it forecast the future.

Concretely: hold back the most recent chunk of your data, say the last three months. Run your method using only the data before that point, exactly as you would have at the time. Compare its three forecasts with the three actuals you hid. The comparison is usually summarized as MAPE — mean absolute percentage error.

A tiny example: the method forecast 100 and 120 for two months; actuals were 110 and 115. The errors are |100-110| / 110 = 9.09% and |120-115| / 115 = 4.35%, so MAPE is about 6.7%. If the method's MAPE on held-out data is 6.7%, a future forecast of 1,000 should be read as 'about 1,000, typically within 7% either way' — and a method with a 30% backtest MAPE shouldn't be quoted to one decimal place, whatever the spreadsheet says.

Backtesting also exposes bias, which MAPE alone hides. If all three held-out forecasts came in low, the method systematically under-forecasts this series — common with moving averages on growing data — and you can correct for the measured bias instead of discovering it in the actuals.

One discipline matters: never tune the method on the held-out months and then report the improved score as the backtest. The moment you peek, those months stop being evidence about the future and become part of the fitting. Hold out, score honestly, then refit on everything for the real forecast.

Forecasting each quarter from its own year-ago value, grown by the average year-over-year rate — then backtesting on 2026's second half.

Year-over-year growth by quarter is consistent: Q1 +9.95%, Q2 +9.55%, Q3 +10.37%, Q4 +10.20% — an average factor of 1.1002. Applying it to each quarter's own 2026 value (which keeps the seasonal shape intact): Q1 2027 ≈ 4983.906 members, Q2 2027 ≈ 4796.872 — call them 4,984 and 4,797.

Why this beats a single trend line here: your quarters aren't interchangeable. A trend fitted through all eight points would forecast Q1 2027 off Q4 2026's peak and overstate it, then understate Q4. Growing each quarter from itself respects the January/autumn rhythm. The assumption to watch is the growth rate itself — if Q1 2027's actual lands more than a couple of percent under 4,984, the 10% era may be ending, and Q2's forecast should be revised before you spend against it.

How do I tell whether a spike in our sales series is seasonal or a one-off? It changes what I forecast.

Ask one question: has it happened before, at the same time, for the same reason?

Seasonality repeats on a calendar. If December brought in $61,200 two years ago and $63,800 last year, against Novembers of $44,000 and $46,000, that's a seasonal peak: it will very likely happen again this December, at a similar share of the year, and your forecast should build it in — typically by forecasting December from previous Decembers, not from November.

A one-off has a biography instead of a rhythm. A single March at $71,000 in a series that otherwise lives at $45,000–$50,000, explained by one bulk order, a local event, or a competitor's stockout, will not repeat on schedule. If you leave it in the data unadjusted, it corrupts twice: it inflates any average that includes it, and it poisons the growth rate computed across it (the month after a one-off always looks like a collapse).

The working habits: plot or list at least two years before judging any spike — one year cannot distinguish rhythm from accident. Keep a one-line log of known one-offs (the event, the bulk order, the closure) with amounts, so the adjustment is documented rather than vibes. And when you adjust, replace the spiked month with an estimated normal month and say so in the forecast — an adjusted series nobody knows about will be 'corrected' back by the next person.

Rule of thumb: if you can name the calendar reason, it's seasonal; if you can name the specific event, it's a one-off; if you can name neither, treat it as unexplained and keep it out of the trend until it repeats.

My forecasts keep getting quoted back to me as promises. How do I present a forecast so people take it seriously but not literally?

Stop issuing a single number. A point forecast is a claim about the center of a range, and if you don't supply the range, your audience will invent one — usually zero width.

Build the range from your own backtest error. Suppose your method backtests with a MAPE of 6% and your point forecast for next quarter is $250,000. A defensible planning band is roughly twice the backtest error — about +/-12% — giving $220,000 to $280,000. That band isn't a statistical confidence interval and you shouldn't dress it up as one; it's an honesty device calibrated on how wrong this method has actually been on this data.

Then present the three numbers with names and jobs: the point forecast (what you'd budget at if forced to one figure), the low end (what cash planning should survive), and the high end (what capacity planning should be ready for). Different decisions legitimately use different ends — the mistake is making every decision use the same one.

Two more habits protect you. Date and version every forecast, and keep the old ones: a forecast you can compare against the actual next quarter is how the method — and your credibility — improves. And state the assumptions in the same breath as the numbers ('assumes the 10% growth rate holds and no price change'), so that when reality diverges, the conversation is about which assumption broke, not about whether you were 'wrong'.

A forecast presented as a range with a track record gets argued with productively. A forecast presented as a point gets quoted back as a promise — your instinct is right.

Two loan offers for $12,000 over 36 months. Offer A: 5.9% APR, no fees. Offer B: 5.4% APR but a $250 origination fee paid upfront. B's rate is lower — is B cheaper?
Comparing total cost of credit, not the headline rate — the fee has to be counted.

No — B is the more expensive loan wearing a cheaper rate.

Offer A: payment $364.52 a month, and over 36 months you pay $13,123 in total. Cost of credit: about $1,123 of interest, no fees.

Offer B: the lower rate does cut the payment, to $361.81, and the interest over the term falls to about $1,025. But adding the $250 fee brings B's total to $13,275 — roughly $152 MORE than A over the three years.

The intuition: half a percent on $12,000 over three years is worth about $110 of interest, because the balance declines as you pay. A $250 fee charged on day one is worth $250. Fees are paid on the full amount immediately; rate savings accrue on a shrinking balance. On short loans especially, always convert both offers to total cost — payment x months, plus every fee — before letting the APR headline decide.
What's the difference between the interest rate, the APR, and the total cost of a loan? Lenders quote all three.

They're three lenses on the same debt, and each hides something the others show.

The interest rate is the pure price of borrowing: the percentage applied to your balance each period. On $10,000 at 8% over 36 months it produces a payment of about $313.36 and total interest of about $1,281. If a loan had no fees at all, rate and APR would be identical.

The APR is the rate plus the compulsory fees, expressed as a rate. Add a $150 origination fee to that same loan and the APR comes out near 9%, even though the interest rate is still 8% — the APR is telling you the fee makes the credit effectively dearer. APR exists for comparison shopping, and it's the better of the two rates to compare across lenders.

Total cost of credit is the only figure in actual money: every payment you will make, plus every fee, minus the amount you borrowed. For the loan above it's about $1,281 without the fee and about $1,431 with it. Total cost is the number that answers 'what does this debt charge me for existing?' — and it's the one that exposes short-term tricks, because a low rate over a long term can quietly cost more in total than a higher rate paid off sooner.

Working rule: shop with APR, decide with total cost, and treat the bare interest rate as the least informative of the three.

Take a small, fast example: $10,000 at 12% APR over 12 months. The payment is $888.49. In month one, interest is 1% of $10,000 = $100.00, so $788.49 reduces the balance. Two practical consequences follow. First, extra payments do the most damage to total interest when made early, because every dollar of principal removed in month one would have been charged interest eleven more times in this loan — and hundreds more times in a mortgage. Second, if you sell or refinance a few years into a long loan, expect the remaining balance to be stubbornly close to what you borrowed. That's not the bank keeping your money; it's the visible shape of paying for a large balance at the beginning. Judge a loan by its total interest over the time you'll actually hold it, not by the split in month one.

A lender quoted me a monthly payment and I want to check it myself instead of taking it on faith. How does the payment formula actually work?

The formula prices the loan as what it is: a stream of equal payments whose present value equals the amount borrowed.

Each future payment is worth less than its face value today, because money today could earn interest. A payment of P arriving in k months, at monthly rate r, is worth P / (1 + r)^k right now. The lender chooses P so that the discounted values of all n payments sum exactly to the principal. Summing that geometric series and solving for P gives the standard formula:

payment = principal x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n)

Work it once by hand. Borrow $15,000 at 6% (so r = 0.005) over 48 months. (1.005)^48 is about 1.2705, so (1 + r)^-n is about 0.7871, and 1 - 0.7871 = 0.2129. The numerator is 15,000 x 0.005 = 75. Payment = 75 / 0.2129 = about $352.28. If a lender quotes you $352.28, the quote is honest arithmetic. If they quote $365 for the same terms, something else is in the payment — an insurance product, a fee financed into the balance, a different rate — and you've caught it before signing rather than after.

Three checks make this practical. Use the monthly rate (annual rate divided by 12), not the annual one. Make sure n is the number of payments, which for a monthly loan is years x 12. And remember the formula prices the amount actually financed — if fees were rolled into the loan, run it on the higher balance, because that's what you're really borrowing.

What is price elasticity, in plain English, and why do economists make such a fuss about whether it's above or below 1?

Elasticity is a ratio of percentages: how many percent volume changes for each one percent the price changes. Raise the price 10% and lose 15% of volume, and the elasticity is -1.5. It's always negative for ordinary goods — higher price, fewer buyers — so people often quote the size and drop the sign.

The fuss about 1 is because it splits the world in two. Work an example. A stall sells at $20 and moves 500 units — $10,000 of revenue. It raises the price 10% to $22.

If elasticity is -0.5 (inelastic), volume falls 5% to 475, and revenue rises to $10,450. The price rise wins: customers grumble and pay.

If elasticity is -1.5 (elastic), volume falls 15% to 425, and revenue falls to $9,350. The same 10% rise loses money, because the volume response outweighs the price gain. At exactly -1, revenue doesn't move at all — the two effects cancel.

What makes a product elastic or not is mostly substitutability and necessity. Insulin, a unique craft product, the only plumber available tonight: inelastic. One brand of cola among six, a gadget with a rival $5 cheaper: elastic. Two warnings before you use the number, though. Elasticity is not a property of the product alone — it depends on the size of the change (a 2% rise and a 40% rise meet different customers) and on the starting price. And it's almost never measured precisely for a small business; treat it as a scenario dial ('what if we're at -0.8? at -2?') rather than a fact about your customers.

The bundle only wins if new adopters outnumber the leak: each adopter adds $30, each switcher costs $9, so you need at least 90 new adopters (attach rising from 30% to about 39%) to break even. Our '20% off everything' weekends are our biggest revenue weekends of the month. My partner wants more of them. Talk me through the downside.

The revenue graph is real and the conclusion is still probably wrong, because revenue is the wrong lens for a discount. Run a representative weekend in margin terms.

Normal weekend: $18,000 of sales at a 45% gross margin — $8,100 of gross profit. Promo weekend: sales jump 30% to $23,400, your biggest weekend. But every item is 20% off while its cost is unchanged. Where a unit sold for $100 with $55 of cost ($45 margin), it now sells for $80 with the same $55 cost — a $25 margin, which is 31.25% of the discounted price. The weekend's gross profit: $23,400 x 31.25% = $7,312.50. You sold 30% more and kept about $790 LESS profit, before counting the extra staff hours the crowd required.

Then the second-order effects compound it. Some of that 30% lift is pull-forward: customers who would have bought next weekend at full price bought this weekend at 20% off, so the following weekend dips. And regulars learn the rhythm — why buy on the 8th if the 22nd is predictably 20% off? Each repeated promotion trains a larger share of your base to wait, so the 'normal' weekends erode and the promos have to deepen to hit the same graph. That's the spiral: the discount stops being an event and becomes your actual price, with the margin of a discount store and the cost base of a full-price one.

Discounts have legitimate jobs — clearing perishable or end-of-line stock whose alternative is a write-off, acquiring genuinely new customers with a measured repeat rate, filling genuinely idle capacity. 'Biggest revenue weekend' is not on the list. Judge the next promo on contribution and on what the two following weekends do, and let your partner's graph include those lines.

I run a one-day workshop. Fixed costs are $3,900 a session (venue, my fee, insurance). I can seat 260 people; materials and refreshments cost $22 a head. What's the lowest ticket price that breaks even on a full house, and what does a $45 ticket do?
Deriving the break-even price from required contribution per seat, then evaluating the $45 ticket.

On a full house of 260, each seat must contribute $15 toward the $3,900 of fixed costs. Add the $22 per-head cost and the break-even ticket is $37 — at $37 a full house exactly covers its costs, and every seat below capacity pushes the true break-even price up (at 200 seats you'd need $41.50).

At a $45 ticket: contribution per seat is $23, a full house contributes $5,980, and profit is $2080. Equally useful: at $45 you break even at 170 seats, so you can sell barely two-thirds of the room and still cover costs.

Framing for your pricing decision: the $37 figure is a floor built on a sellout, which is the most fragile assumption in the building. The $45 ticket buys you a 90-seat cushion against a disappointing house. Price for the attendance you can defend, not the attendance you hope for — and if you discount, discount from $45 knowing each $1 off raises the break-even headcount by roughly 8 seats at the margin.
When we model a price cut, sales always targets 'the volume needed to keep revenue flat'. Something about that feels off. Is it?

Your instinct is right — revenue-flat is the wrong target, and it systematically flatters price cuts.

Numbers make it plain. A product sells at $50, costs $30 a unit, and moves 1,000 units a month: revenue $50,000, contribution $20,000. You cut the price 10% to $45.

Revenue-flat volume: $50,000 / $45 = 1,112 units (up 11.1%). Hit exactly that and the dashboard shows revenue unchanged — success. But each unit now contributes $15 instead of $20, so contribution is 1,112 x $15 = $16,680. You're $3,320 a month worse off while the revenue line says nothing happened.

Profit-flat volume: $20,000 / $15 = 1,334 units (up 33.3%) — three times the growth the revenue target demanded. The reason is structural: the price cut comes entirely out of the $20 margin, not out of the $50 price, so margin falls 25% when price falls 10%. Any volume target computed on revenue inherits the smaller, easier number.

The same trap runs in reverse on price rises: a rise can lose revenue and still gain profit, and a revenue-targeted review will call it a failure. Retire the revenue target for pricing decisions. The question is never 'how much volume keeps the top line flat?' — it's 'how much volume keeps contribution flat, and do we believe we'll get it?'

Why do you always ask whether a table has 'total rows' in it before summing it? Isn't a total just another number?

Because a total row is the one row in a table that is guaranteed to corrupt a sum, silently and at scale.

Picture the export: ninety-nine sales rows and, at the bottom, the spreadsheet's own TOTAL row — same columns, amount equal to the sum of everything above it. It imports beautifully, because structurally it looks like data. Now SUM the amount column and you get every sale counted twice: the true total plus the total. If the true figure was $48,000, your report says $96,000, and nothing in the output looks wrong — there's no error message for arithmetic that succeeded on the wrong rows.

Worse, the stored total is usually stale or defective in its own right: it was computed by the spreadsheet from whatever rows existed then, including any duplicates and sign errors, so it can't serve as an independent check on the detail. Comparing your sum against it just compares the data with its own shadow.

Three habits neutralize the whole class of problem. Filter before you sum: if the table has any kind of row marker, use it; if not, look for the fingerprints — a row whose label says TOTAL, a blank date, an amount equal to the sum of the others. Keep a control total from an independent source (the bank, the POS daily report) and reconcile against that instead. And count rows: if the source system says 412 transactions and your table has 413 rows, the extra row is a question that answers itself.

A total is a conclusion, not an observation. The moment it sits in the data wearing the same shape as the observations, every aggregate downstream is suspect.

Half our refunds get entered as positive numbers and half as negative, depending on who typed them. Does it really matter if the totals are 'about right'?

It matters more than almost anything else in a small ledger, because a sign error is worth double the transaction. A $150 refund entered as +150 instead of -150 doesn't move your total by $150 — it moves it by $300: the $150 that should have left, plus the $150 that wrongly arrived. Three such refunds in a month and your figures are $900 adrift, in the flattering direction, which is why sign errors survive: nobody audits good news.

'About right' is also doing heavy lifting. Totals built from inconsistently signed rows aren't approximately right; they're right only when the errors happen to cancel, which is luck wearing a pattern. The same month's data summed by two people — one who filters refunds out first, one who doesn't — gives two different answers, and both can defend their method.

The fix is boring and total: one written convention (money in positive, money out negative — refunds, reversals, credit notes, and chargebacks are money out), applied at entry, ideally enforced by the form rather than by memory. A 'refund' type that always stores negative removes the human choice entirely. Then add the cheap detective control: search the table for rows whose description says refund, reversal, or credit while the amount is positive. In a healthy table that query returns nothing. Run it monthly; it's the highest-value two minutes in small-business bookkeeping.

How do I know my sales table is right? I can check it against itself forever and it always agrees with itself.

That's exactly the trap: internal consistency proves only that the table agrees with its own assumptions. The check that means something is reconciliation against an independent source — records created by a different process that can't share the table's errors. For sales, the classic independent source is the bank.

Work it once. Your table says October receipts were $48,290. Card settlements and deposits at the bank say $47,940 actually arrived. The gap is $350. Now the gap itself becomes the clue, because different defects leave differently shaped gaps:

- A gap equal to exactly one transaction suggests a missing or duplicated row.
- A gap equal to TWICE a transaction is the signature of a sign error: a $175 refund recorded as +$175 instead of -$175 makes the books $350 richer than the bank. ($350 is twice $175 — look for a $175 refund first.)
- A small, ragged gap that matches nothing is usually timing: a settlement that landed November 1 for an October sale.

Reconcile monthly, while the gap is small enough to interrogate. A $350 gap in October is an afternoon's detective work; the same habit skipped for a year becomes a $20,000 gap that no longer decomposes into findable pieces. And keep the direction of trust straight: when the table and the bank disagree, the bank is describing money that moved, while the table is describing money someone typed. Start by believing the bank and make the table explain itself.

What's the right way to round working hours for payroll? Our clock app records exact minutes and payroll is a mess of long decimals.

Round the shifts, not the totals, to a stated increment — the nearest quarter hour is the common choice — and apply it the same way every time. Three principles make a rounding policy defensible:

1. Round each shift before summing. A shift is the unit a person actually worked and can verify. Rounding only the weekly total leaves every daily figure in dispute and can quietly move someone across an overtime threshold: 40.03 raw hours is overtime; five shifts that each round to exactly 8.00 is a 40.00-hour week with none. Which answer you get should come from the policy, not from where the rounding happened to be applied.

2. Round to NEAREST, never always down (or always up). Always-down is a slow skim — two or three minutes a shift is an hour a month per person — and always-up is a slow leak. Nearest is symmetric: over a month, the gains and losses roughly cancel for everyone, and you can demonstrate that from the data if ever asked.

3. Write it down and keep the raw times. The policy (increment, nearest, per-shift) belongs in the handbook, and the unrounded clock records should be retained — they're the audit trail that proves the rounded figures were produced by the rule rather than by someone's judgment on the day.

One more practical point: pick an increment your payroll arithmetic handles cleanly. Quarter hours (.00/.25/.50/.75) multiply exactly; tenths (.1 steps) invite floating-point dust like 37.749999 hours into reports, and someone will eventually 'fix' a correct figure that merely looks wrong.

If I put someone on salary, I don't have to worry about overtime for them anymore, right? Salary means exempt, doesn't it?

No — and this is one of the most expensive misconceptions in small-business payroll. 'Salaried' describes how pay is calculated. 'Exempt' describes a legal classification. They're independent choices, and neither implies the other.

A salaried employee can be non-exempt: paid a fixed weekly amount, but still owed overtime for hours over the threshold in your jurisdiction, with the salary converted to an implied hourly rate for the calculation (a $1,040 weekly salary for a 40-hour week implies $26/h, so overtime hours price at $39). Conversely, some hourly-paid roles can sit in exempt categories. What decides exemption is the actual duties of the job and the rules where you operate — not the pay method, not the job title, and not what the offer letter calls it.

The payroll-math consequence: if you stop tracking hours when someone goes on salary, you destroy the very data you'd need if their classification were ever questioned. Back-overtime claims are computed from hours; with no records, estimates replace them, and estimates rarely favor the employer. Keep recording hours for salaried staff even when this week's pay doesn't depend on them.

Practical rule: treat classification as a decision to make deliberately — duties first, then pay method — and check it against your local labor rules or an employment adviser before relying on it. The cost of asking once is trivial next to the cost of reclassifying two years of payroll retroactively.

Our payroll provider gives us a summary each period and I've been checking the summary against last period's summary. My accountant says that's not really checking. What should I do instead?

Your accountant is right: comparing one summary with another only proves the numbers didn't change much — and a wrong rate, applied consistently, produces summaries that agree beautifully while being wrong every single period. A systematic error is invisible to trend checks precisely because it's systematic.

Real checking is recomputation from source. Payroll's sources are the shift records, the rate table, and the stated rules (overtime threshold, rounding, differentials). Once a period — monthly is enough — rebuild the payroll from those rows with your own query and compare person by person against what was paid. You're not looking for a matching total; you're looking for the handful of people who differ, because differences have causes: a raise entered a week late, a shift priced under the old rate, hours approved after the file was built.

Calibrate expectations: on a healthy payroll, recomputation usually finds zero or a few small differences — say two people and $31.50 on a $9,400 payroll. That is not a failure of the check; that IS the check working. The money is trivial; the signal is that your rate table and your provider's now agree, and the two exceptions get names and reasons instead of compounding silently into a grievance or an audit finding.

The general principle travels: any figure that arrives as a summary should occasionally be rebuilt from its rows. Summaries are where errors go to become permanent.

I send my partners a monthly numbers summary and nobody reads past the first line. What does a numbers report that people actually read look like?

Short, in a fixed order, and honest about what it doesn't know. The structure that works:

1. One headline figure with its comparison. 'Profit $34,360, up from $30,130 last month.' Not six KPIs — one number that answers 'how did we do?', with the period it beats or misses.

2. The three biggest movements, each with a cause or an explicit 'unexplained'. Partners don't need every line; they need to know the month's story is understood. A variance with a sourced explanation builds trust; a variance flagged as unexplained builds more, because it proves the explained ones were actually checked.

3. A projection with its assumptions attached. 'November ≈ $32,300 profit, assuming collections dip 2% for holiday weeks.' A projection without assumptions is a promise; with them, it's a tool — readers can argue with the assumption, which is the productive argument.

4. A data-quality note whenever one is earned. 'A duplicate import overstated sales by $11,240; corrected figures throughout.' Burying a correction teaches readers to distrust every future report; leading with it teaches them the numbers are audited.

5. Decisions needed, if any, stated as decisions. 'Approve the repairs budget line' — not a paragraph of context hoping someone infers it.

What to cut: every line that didn't move, every figure without a comparison, and every adjective. A report people finish is one page of numbers that each earn their place — and the discipline of recomputing each figure fresh each month, rather than editing last month's file, is what keeps it true.

When I write the monthly report there's always one variance I can't explain, and I feel pressure to put SOMETHING — 'probably seasonal' — rather than leave a blank. Is that actually a problem?

Yes, and it's one of the quiet ways reports become fiction. 'Probably seasonal' is not an explanation; it's a sedative. It tells every reader the variance was understood when it wasn't, and it closes the file — nobody investigates a line that's already labeled.

The pattern repeats everywhere: a supplies line creeps $600 in a month and gets waved at 'growth'; three quarters later the accumulated 'growth' is five figures and turns out to be a duplicated vendor payment, a mis-keyed rate, or stock walking away. Almost every real bookkeeping problem first appears as a small unexplained variance wearing a plausible label.

Write 'UNEXPLAINED — checking' instead, with the amount and the line. It does three things a guess can't. It keeps the question open, so next month someone (often you) actually looks. It protects the credibility of everything else in the report — readers who see one honest flag trust the ten explained lines more, not less. And it creates a record: if the same line is unexplained three months running, the report itself escalates it from a footnote to a finding.

There's a fairness point too. A guessed explanation often quietly accuses someone — 'probably the new hire's training waste' — without evidence. 'Unexplained' accuses no one. Explain what you can source, flag what you can't, and let the flag do its work.

Every month I copy last month's report file, update the numbers, and send it. Faster than starting fresh. Any reason to change?

One big one: a copied report inherits last month's errors with this month's authority. The classic case is the spreadsheet range that stops one row short — the SUM covers rows 2–40, a new category arrives in row 41, and for five months the report understates expenses by that category while looking identical in form to the correct reports before it. Copying doesn't just preserve mistakes; it preserves them invisibly, because the format's familiarity stops you reading the figures as new claims.

Recomputing fresh — pulling this month's rows and deriving every figure in the report from them — costs minutes with a query and buys three things. The figures are this month's, all of them, including the ones you'd have sworn didn't change. New rows and categories surface immediately instead of hiding outside a stale range. And the report gains an audit trail: each number traces to rows you can show, not to a cell whose formula nobody has read since spring.

Keep the template for the WORDS — the structure, the headings, the order readers expect. Recompute the NUMBERS. The right unit to carry forward is the question the report answers, never the answer itself.
